doc.title: Bob Hardaway interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: Becoming a multi-doubler: flute, oboe and NBC staff orchestra
summary: Unable to get studio work at 30, he took up flute and oboe together and two years later won a staff job at NBC as oboe doubler. He ended up with a full set of flutes, English horn and clarinets.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: So were you establishing a career off the road in the L.A. area?

Yeah, I played the clarinet and the saxophone, and by the time I was 30 I felt, having heard a lot of players, that I could play at a par with them, but I wasn’t getting any of the good work in town, the studio work. And I was trying to figure out why. So I decided maybe I’d do better if I became a multi-doubler. So I was 30 at the time and I took up both the flute and the oboe at the same time, and really applied myself to them. And two years later I got a job on the staff orchestra at NBC, they still had a staff orchestra then, that was in the early 60s, as the oboe doubler. And I ended up having it all. I had all the flutes, the piccolo, the alto flute, the C flute, the bass flute.
Oh, you even had a bass flute.

The bass flute. I still have it but I’ve used it four times or something. That was because of, well let’s see who was it, Mancini was the one that made — Hank Mancini was the one that made the alto flute popular, and so everybody had to have an alto flute then. And then he may also have been the one that used the bass flute maybe. I don’t remember. But anyway I also had the English horn and the oboe, and the clarinet and the bass clarinet, and all the saxophones.
